title: The Puzzles You Can Still Beat AI At
hook: Mental rotation, tricky logic riddles, Tower of Hanoi past six discs — humans still win. The failures aren't random; they map the difference between pattern-matching and reasoning.
key_points: Models struggle with mental rotation and other spatial-reasoning tasks, per MIT Technology Review.
On ARC-AGI-style visual puzzles they've improved a lot in a year, but some still stump them.
Classic step-by-step puzzles (Tower of Hanoi, river crossings) break down once complexity passes roughly six elements.
Slightly altered Knights-and-Knaves riddles trip up models that memorized the standard version.
Tell: models often do better when the same puzzle is given as numbers instead of a picture.
content_html: Puzzles have been AI's measuring stick since the beginning — the term "machine learning" was popularized in a 1959 paper by IBM's Arthur Samuel, who taught a computer to play checkers. MIT Technology Review's roundup of puzzles that today's frontier models still flub is a nice reminder that the measuring stick hasn't stopped being useful, and that you can personally still beat the state of the art at several things.
extra_html:
The pattern in the failures is more interesting than any single failure. Spatial reasoning is a weak spot: ask a model to mentally rotate a 3D object and identify it from a new angle and it often gets lost, even though it can describe an image fluently. On abstract visual puzzles in the ARC-AGI family, models have improved sharply over the past year, yet some remain unsolved. Give a model a Knights-and-Knaves logic riddle with a subtle variation from the textbook version and it may answer the version it memorized. And on puzzles that require executing many dependent steps — Tower of Hanoi, river crossings, logic grids — performance degrades once you get past roughly six elements.

The most telling detail: models frequently do better when the same puzzle is handed to them as strings of numbers rather than as a picture. That points away from "it can't reason" and toward something narrower and more useful to know — the visual and spatial representation is the bottleneck, and a lot of apparent reasoning rests on having seen the pattern before. It's the practical version of the whole hype question. Not "is it smart?" but "smart at what, represented how?"

related.title: What AI Can't Do
related.hook: Today's AI can write a sonnet and flunk a question a child gets right. Knowing its hard edges — no real understanding, no live truth, no common sense — is what makes you good at using it.

related.title: Hype or Real?
related.hook: AI coverage swings between 'this changes everything' and 'it's all a bubble.' The truth is usually in between — and a few questions help you judge any big AI claim for yourself.

related.title: AI That Sees & Hears
related.hook: Early chatbots only read and wrote text. Today's AI is 'multimodal' — one system can look at a photo, listen to your voice, and reply in words or pictures, the way people switch senses.

flashcards.prompt: Why does a small twist on a familiar logic riddle often break a model?

choices.text: It may be recalling the memorized standard version instead of reasoning through this one
Riddles are always outside a model's training data

flashcards.explanation_html: The model has seen the classic puzzle many times. When the variant looks almost identical, pattern-matching to the remembered answer beats noticing the change.

flashcards.prompt: What's the clue in models doing better on a puzzle given as numbers than as an image?
flashcards.back_html: It suggests the weakness is in visual and spatial representation, not the logic itself — the same problem is solvable once it arrives in a form the model handles well.

flashcards.prompt: What happens to models on step-by-step puzzles like Tower of Hanoi as size grows?

choices.text: They cope with small cases and fall apart once complexity rises past a handful of elements
They solve any size instantly, since the rules are simple
They refuse to attempt the puzzle at all

flashcards.explanation_html: The rules are trivial; executing many dependent steps without losing track is not. Reported breakdowns start around six or more elements.
